task.title: Match a small regular expression language
task.statement:
Write a JavaScript function `regexMatch(pattern, text)` that returns `true` when the whole of `text` matches `pattern`, `false` when it does not, and `null` when `pattern` is not valid in the language below or either argument is not a string. Inputs are ASCII.

The language:
- Special characters outside a class are `\ . [ ( ) | * + ? { }`. Every other character, including `]`, `^`, `$` and `-`, matches itself.
- `.` matches any one character, newline included.
- `\d` matches 0-9, `\w` matches A-Z, a-z, 0-9 and `_`, `\s` matches space, tab, \n, \r, \f and \v. A backslash before any other character matches that character literally: `\n` matches the letter `n`, `\.` a dot, `\\` a backslash. A pattern that ends in a lone backslash is invalid.
- `(` ... `)` groups. Groups may be empty, and so may alternatives: `()`, `a|` and `|` are valid and match the empty string. Unbalanced parentheses are invalid. There is no other group syntax, so `(?:a)` is invalid.
- `|` is alternation with the lowest precedence. The whole pattern must match the whole text.
- Quantifiers `*`, `+`, `?`, `{m}`, `{m,}` and `{m,n}` apply to the atom just before them. `m` and `n` are decimal digits with values up to 1000 and `n` must not be less than `m`. A quantifier with nothing to repeat (at the start, after `(` or `|`) is invalid, and so is a quantifier directly after another one (`a**`, `a+?`, `a{2}*`). A `{` that does not begin a valid quantifier (`a{`, `a{,2}`, `a{1,x}`) and any `}` outside a quantifier are invalid.
- `[` ... `]` is a class, `[^` ... `]` a negated class; it matches one character. Inside a class only `\` and `]` are special: `]` closes it, and `\` escapes exactly as outside (`\]` is a literal `]`, `\d`, `\w`, `\s` add their sets). A class must contain at least one item, so `[]` and `[^]` are invalid; an unterminated class is invalid. An item followed by `-` and another single-character item forms a range, which is invalid if its end is below its start (`[z-a]`) or either end is a `\d`, `\w` or `\s` set on the right (`[a-\d]`). A `-` that does not form a range is literal: `[-a]`, `[a-]`, `[a-c-e]` (a, b, c, `-`, e) and `[\d-z]` (digits, `-`, z).
